title: “Monks, suppose a man is struck by an arrow, and then they strike him with a second arrow. Thus, monks, that man experiences the feeling…
content: “Monks, suppose a man is struck by an arrow, and then they strike him with a second arrow. Thus, monks, that man experiences the feeling of both arrows. So too, monks, an untaught ordinary person, when touched by a painful feeling, sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. He experiences two feelings — a bodily feeling and a mental feeling. Touched by that painful feeling, he feels aversion. Because he feels aversion toward that painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling persists. Touched by that painful feeling, he delights in sensual pleasures. Why? Because, monks, the untaught ordinary person knows no escape from painful feeling other than sensual pleasure. Delighting in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling persists. He does not know as it actually is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding these feelings. Not knowing as it actually is the origination … and escape regarding these feelings, the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling persists. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. This, monks, is called an untaught ordinary person who is bound by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is bound by suffering.”

title: “Here, brahmin, a person is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not…
content: “Here, brahmin, a person is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever, not free from craving. Then a severe illness arises for him. Affected by that severe illness, he thinks: ‘Truly, agreeable sensual pleasures will leave me,’ or ‘I will leave agreeable sensual pleasures.’ He sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. This, brahmin, is a person who is subject to death, fearful, and falls into terror at the thought of death.”

title: “Monks, suppose a person is being swept away by a river that is lovely and pleasant. A man with good eyesight, standing on the bank,…
content: “Monks, suppose a person is being swept away by a river that is lovely and pleasant. A man with good eyesight, standing on the bank, seeing him, says: ‘Good man, though you are being swept away by this lovely, pleasant river, further down there is a lake with waves and whirlpools, with crocodiles and demons. If you reach that place, you will die or suffer deadly pain.’ Then that person, hearing his words, struggles upstream with his hands and feet. Monks, I have given this simile to make the meaning clear. The meaning here is this: ‘The river,’ monks, is a synonym for craving. ‘Lovely and pleasant’ is a synonym for the six internal sense bases. ‘The lake further down’ is a synonym for the five lower fetters. ‘Waves’ is a synonym for anger and distress. ‘Whirlpools’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Crocodiles and demons’ is a synonym for women. ‘Struggling upstream’ is a synonym for renunciation. ‘Struggling with hands and feet’ is a synonym for arousing energy. ‘The man with good eyesight standing on the bank’ is a synonym for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”

title: O monks, these six sense bases — Where they are unrestrained, There suffering comes to be. Those who learn to guard them, To restrain and…
content:
O monks, these six sense bases —
Where they are unrestrained,
There suffering comes to be.
Those who learn to guard them,
To restrain and protect them,
With faith as their companion,
Dwell freed from sensual lust.

Seeing forms that are pleasing,
Seeing forms that are displeasing,
Restrain the path of lust
For forms that are pleasing —
Do not let the mind be defiled,
Thinking: ‘I do not delight in forms.’

Having heard sounds —
Pleasing and displeasing,
Do not be infatuated with pleasing sounds.
Restrain the mind’s aversion
For sounds that are displeasing,
Do not let the mind be defiled,
Thinking: ‘I do not delight in sounds.’

Having smelled fragrant, delightful odors,
Having smelled foul, loathsome odors —
Restrain aversion for loathsome odors,
And for delightful ones,
Do not let desire dominate.

Having tasted sweet flavors,
And also flavors that are not sweet,
Do not develop greed
When enjoying a sweet taste,
Do not utter words of opposition
When tasting what is not sweet.

When touched by pleasant contact,
Do not be infatuated with lust;
When touched by painful contact,
Do not be violently shaken.
For both contacts — pleasant and painful —
Remain equanimous,
Without approval or opposition,
Whatever contact may arise.

Those who follow proliferated perceptions,
Who are lost in conceptual proliferation,
Who act upon false thoughts —
Abandon all household activities
Born of the mind,
Practice restraint in your actions,
Directing yourself to the path of seclusion.

Thus, with the mind well-developed
Regarding these six sense bases,
Whatever contact occurs,
The mind is not disturbed.
Having subdued both greed and hatred,
O monk, go to the far shore,
Beyond the bonds of birth and death.

title: “Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises…
content: “Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then because he delights, praises, and dwells with lust, delight arises. With the arising of delight, lust arises. With the arising of lust, bondage arises. Bound by the bondage of delight, Migajāla, that monk is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’ Even if he lives in remote lodgings, in forests, in groves, in quiet places, with little sound, little noise, free from people’s breath, secluded, suitable for seclusion — still he is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’ Why? Because craving, the companion, has not been abandoned by him. Therefore he is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’”

title: “Monks, if one does not intend, does not plan, and has no tendency towards anything, there is no basis for the establishment of consciousness. When…
content: “Monks, if one does not intend, does not plan, and has no tendency towards anything, there is no basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is no basis, consciousness does not become established. When consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no production of future renewed existence. When there is no future renewed existence, future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”

title: “And, Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise…
content: “And, Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them, then because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, delight ceases. With the cessation of delight, lust ceases. With the cessation of lust, bondage ceases. Not being bound by the bondage of delight, Migajāla, that monk is called ‘one who dwells alone.’”

title: “Monks, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are fetters — greed is not abandoned, hatred is not abandoned, delusion is not abandoned. Because…
content: “Monks, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are fetters — greed is not abandoned, hatred is not abandoned, delusion is not abandoned. Because greed, hatred, and delusion are not abandoned, he is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is not freed from suffering.”

title: “When, monks, a monk is not lustful regarding objects that can provoke lust, and his self is free from lust; is not hateful regarding objects…
content: “When, monks, a monk is not lustful regarding objects that can provoke lust, and his self is free from lust; is not hateful regarding objects that can provoke hatred, and his self is free from hatred; is not deluded regarding objects that can provoke delusion, and his self is free from delusion; is not infatuated regarding objects that can provoke infatuation, and his self is free from infatuation — then he has no fear, no trembling, no terror, does not fall into fear, and does not go by whatever ascetics may say.”

title: “Monk, I say that there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These three feelings have been spoken of by me. But,…
content: “Monk, I say that there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These three feelings have been spoken of by me. But, monk, I also say: ‘Whatever is felt is included in suffering.’ It is in relation to the impermanence of formations that this is said: ‘Whatever is felt is included in suffering.’ It is in relation to the nature of destruction, the nature of vanishing, the nature of fading away, the nature of cessation, the nature of change of formations that this is said: ‘Whatever is felt is included in suffering.’”
